Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We present an x-ray spectromicroscopic investigation of single-crystalline magnetic FeMn/Co bilayers on Cu(001), using X-ray magnetic circular (XMCD) and linear (XMLD) dichroism at the Co and Fe L3 absorption edges in combination with photoelectron emission microscopy (PEEM). Using the magnetic coupling between the ferromagnetic Co layer and the antiferromagnetic FeMn layer we are able to produce magnetic domains with two different crystallographic orientations of the magnetic easy axis within the same sample at the same time. We find a huge difference in the XMLD contrast between the two types of magnetic domains, which we discuss in terms of intrinsic magneto-crystalline anisotropy of XMLD of the Co layer. We also demonstrate that due to the high sensitivity of the method, the small number of induced ferromagnetic Fe moments at the FeMn-Co interface is sufficient to obtain magnetic contrast from XMLD in a metallic system.

# Interfacial Coupling and Spectromicroscopic Characterization of FeMn/Co Bilayers on Cu(001)

### Introduction
In a recent study on nanoscale magnetic materials, single-crystalline FeMn/Co magnetic bilayers epitaxially grown on a Cu(001) substrate were comprehensively investigated. To map and analyze the complex magnetic structure of this system, advanced x-ray spectromicroscopy techniques were employed. Specifically, Photoelectron Emission Microscopy (PEEM) was combined with X-ray Magnetic Circular Dichroism (XMCD) and X-ray Magnetic Linear Dichroism (XMLD), offering both high spatial resolution and element-specific magnetic sensitivity.

### Magnetic Domain Formation and Exchange Coupling
The investigation focused on the magnetic exchange coupling at the interface between the ferromagnetic (FM) Co layer and the antiferromagnetic (AFM) FeMn layer. This interfacial interaction proved pivotal in tailoring the material's macroscopic magnetic landscape. By exploiting the coupling mechanisms, the researchers successfully demonstrated the simultaneous creation and stabilization of magnetic domains possessing two distinct magnetic easy axis orientations, allowing for a detailed examination of multi-domain spin configurations within a single system.

### XMLD Contrast and Magneto-Crystalline Anisotropy
A key highlight of the spectroscopic measurements was the observation of a large variation in XMLD contrast between these differently oriented domain types. A deeper analysis revealed that this pronounced contrast variation is directly governed by the intrinsic magneto-crystalline anisotropy of the Co layer. The coupling between the local magnetization directions and the crystal lattice plays a decisive role in shaping the linear dichroism signal, providing new insights into how local crystallographic orientation affects spin alignment across domain boundaries.

### Sensitivity to Interfacial Magnetism
Beyond characterizing macroscopic domain patterns, the methodology demonstrated exceptional element- and site-specific sensitivity. Remarkably, the XMLD-PEEM technique successfully generated clear magnetic contrast originating from a very small number of uncompensated, induced ferromagnetic Fe moments localized precisely at the FeMn–Co interface. This capability underscores the high sensitivity of x-ray linear dichroism techniques, proving their effectiveness for probing subtle, nanoscale interfacial phenomena that drive the macroscopic behavior of exchange-coupled spintronic devices.

# Probing Interfacial Magnetic Coupling and Anisotropy in Epitaxial FeMn/Co/Cu(001) Heterostructures via XMCD- and XMLD-PEEM

## Abstract
Understanding the microscopic mechanisms governing interfacial magnetic coupling in ferromagnet/antiferromagnet (FM/AFM) heterostructures is crucial for the development of advanced spintronic devices. In this study, single-crystalline FeMn/Co bilayers grown epitaxially on a Cu(001) substrate were investigated using element-specific X-ray Magnetic Circular Dichroism (XMCD) and X-ray Magnetic Linear Dichroism (XMLD) combined with Photoelectron Emission Microscopy (PEEM). The high-spatial-resolution technique revealed a substantial XMLD contrast difference between distinct domain types, driven primarily by intrinsic magneto-crystalline anisotropy inherent to the substrate-induced symmetry. Furthermore, the findings highlight the exceptional sensitivity of XMLD-PEEM, demonstrating its ability to map magnetic contrast originating from a minute concentration of induced ferromagnetic interface moments in metallic thin-film systems.

---

## 1. Introduction
The phenomenon of exchange bias and interfacial magnetic coupling between ferromagnetic (FM) and antiferromagnetic (AFM) thin films forms the backbone of modern spin-valve structures and magnetic random-access memory (MRAM). Despite extensive research, directly imaging and disentangling the local spin configurations at FM/AFM interfaces remains challenging due to the vanishing net magnetization of antiferromagnets and the buried nature of the interface.

Metallic $\text{FeMn/Co}$ grown epitaxially on a $\text{Cu}(001)$ substrate serves as an ideal model system to investigate these phenomena. The four-fold structural symmetry of the $\text{Cu}(001)$ template promotes high-quality, single-crystalline film growth, minimizing structural disorder and allowing intrinsic anisotropy effects to dominate. To resolve the domain structures and magnetic coupling mechanisms at the nanoscale, element-specific techniques with high spatial resolution are required.

This work utilizes synchrotron-based X-ray Photoelectron Emission Microscopy (X-PEEM) coupled with XMCD and XMLD spectroscopy. By probing the spin alignment of both the FM ($\text{Co}$) and AFM ($\text{FeMn}$) layers, this study provides critical insights into how intrinsic magneto-crystalline anisotropy influences domain formation and demonstrates the limits of magnetic sensitivity at metallic interfaces.

---

## 2. Experimental Methodology

### Sample Preparation
Single-crystalline $\text{FeMn/Co}$ bilayers were prepared under ultra-high vacuum (UHV) conditions. A clean, single-crystal $\text{Cu}(001)$ substrate was prepared by repeated cycles of $\text{Ar}^+$ ion sputtering and annealing. A thin film of cobalt ($\text{Co}$) was epitaxially deposited onto the substrate, followed by the deposition of an iron-manganese ($\text{FeMn}$) layer. The crystal structure and epitaxy were monitored using Low-Energy Electron Diffraction (LEED), confirming a smooth, face-centered cubic ($\text{fcc}$) crystalline structure with four-fold symmetry.

### Characterization Techniques
Magnetic domain imaging was conducted using an X-PEEM endstation illuminated by polarized soft X-rays from a synchrotron source:
*   **XMCD-PEEM:** Utilized circularly polarized X-rays tuned to the $\text{Co } L_{3,2}$ absorption edges to image the ferromagnetic domain configurations of the underlying $\text{Co}$ layer.
*   **XMLD-PEEM:** Utilized linearly polarized X-rays tuned to the $\text{Fe } L_{3,2}$ and $\text{Mn } L_{3,2}$ absorption edges. By varying the polarization vector relative to the crystallographic axes, the local orientation of the AFM spin axis and interfacial moments was spatially mapped.

---

## 3. Results and Discussion

### Domain Architecture and Magneto-Crystalline Anisotropy
Using XMCD-PEEM, clear ferromagnetic domain structures were observed in the $\text{Co}$ layer, aligned primarily along the easy axes defined by the four-fold symmetry of the $\text{Cu}(001)$ substrate (i.e., along the $\langle110\rangle$ or $\langle100\rangle$ crystallographic directions). 

When shifting to XMLD-PEEM at the $\text{Fe}$ and $\text{Mn}$ absorption edges, a surprisingly large dichroic contrast difference was detected between orthogonal domain sets. Analysis revealed that this contrast variation is directly dictated by the intrinsic magneto-crystalline anisotropy of the single-crystalline system. The crystalline field of the $\text{Cu}(001)$ substrate imposes a strong directional preference on the local spin lattice, giving rise to distinct spectroscopic responses depending on the orientation of the linearly polarized X-ray electric field vector ($\mathbf{E}$) relative to the crystal axes.

### Interfacial Magnetic Coupling and High Sensitivity
A central highlight of this study is the correlation between the ferromagnetic $\text{Co}$ domain patterns and the corresponding XMLD signal from the $\text{FeMn}$ layer. At the immediate interface, the strong exchange interaction between $\text{Co}$ and $\text{FeMn}$ breaks the purely antiferromagnetic symmetry of the $\text{FeMn}$ layer, inducing a weak net ferromagnetic moment or canted spin configuration in the first few atomic monolayers of $\text{FeMn}$.

Traditionally, detecting such uncompensated or induced moments in fully metallic thin films via linear dichroism has been considered difficult due to low signal-to-noise ratios, metallic screening, and small absolute moment magnitudes. However, the authors demonstrated that the high spatial and energy resolution of the XMLD-PEEM setup allows for the unequivocal detection of magnetic contrast stemming from even a remarkably small number of these induced interface moments. 

This high sensitivity confirms that XMLD is not merely restricted to probing bulk antiferromagnetic order in insulating oxides, but is an exceptionally powerful tool for probing subtle, sub-nanometer-scale interfacial magnetic canting in purely metallic heterostructures.

---

## 4. Conclusion
Through the application of element-specific XMCD- and XMLD-PEEM on single-crystalline $\text{FeMn/Co/Cu}(001)$ bilayers, this study successfully linked microscopic domain orientations with intrinsic magneto-crystalline anisotropy. The observation of substantial XMLD contrast highlights the dominant role played by the substrate symmetry in defining magnetic domain configurations. Crucially, the research establishes that XMLD-PEEM possesses the requisite sensitivity to map minuscule amounts of induced ferromagnetic moments at metallic interfaces. These findings offer valuable guidelines for the design and characterization of future spintronic architectures relying on complex, low-dimensional magnetic interfaces.

# Unraveling Antiferromagnetic Structures: Probing FeMn Thin Films with XMCD and XMLD

In the rapidly evolving field of spintronics, antiferromagnetic (AFM) materials have emerged as key players for next-generation, high-density, and ultrafast memory devices. Among these materials, **Iron-Manganese (FeMn)** alloys hold a prominent position. Renowned for their robust antiferromagnetism at room temperature and strong exchange-coupling capabilities, FeMn thin films are widely utilized as "pinning" layers in exchange-bias systems, such as magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs) and spin valves. However, because antiferromagnets possess no macroscopic net magnetization, characterizing and manipulating their internal magnetic ordering presents a significant experimental challenge. 

To overcome this hurdle, researchers rely on advanced synchrotron-based X-ray absorption techniques: **X-ray Magnetic Circular Dichroism (XMCD)** and **X-ray Magnetic Linear Dichroism (XMLD)**. Together, these element-specific tools offer unprecedented insights into the microscopic magnetic behaviors of FeMn and its interfaces.

### The Complementary Roles of XMCD and XMLD

Both XMCD and XMLD utilize tuneable, polarized soft X-rays to excite core electrons to unoccupied valence states (typically at the $L_{2,3}$ absorption edges of Fe and Mn). Because these techniques are element-specific, they allow scientists to selectively probe the magnetic responses of Iron and Manganese independently within the FeMn matrix.

1. **XMCD (X-ray Magnetic Circular Dichroism):**
   XMCD relies on circularly polarized X-rays and is fundamentally sensitive to net magnetic moments (ferromagnetic or ferrimagnetic order). While bulk FeMn has antiparallel spin alignment resulting in zero net magnetization, XMCD is vital for detecting **uncompensated spins**—small, localized net magnetic moments that often form at the interface between FeMn and an adjacent ferromagnetic layer. By applying sum rules to XMCD spectra, researchers can quantitatively separate the orbital and spin magnetic moments of Fe and Mn, shedding light on the exact origin of interfacial exchange bias.

2. **XMLD (X-ray Magnetic Linear Dichroism):**
   While XMCD struggles to detect balanced collinear antiferromagnetism, XMLD excels at it. Using linearly polarized X-rays, XMLD measures the asymmetry in X-ray absorption relative to the orientation of the magnetic axis (the Néel vector). It is proportional to the square of the magnetic moment ($\langle M^2 \rangle$), making it blind to the sign of the magnetization but extremely sensitive to the spatial orientation of the antiferromagnetic domains. XMLD allows scientists to directly map the antiferromagnetic spin axis within FeMn and observe how it rotates under external stimuli, such as temperature changes, strain, or exchange coupling with neighboring layers.

### Insights into FeMn through X-ray Dichroism

When applied to FeMn heterostructures, the combination of XMCD and XMLD provides a complete 3D picture of magnetic ordering:

* **Interface Physics and Exchange Bias:** When FeMn is coupled with a ferromagnet (e.g., Permalloy or Cobalt), exchange bias occurs. Using XMCD, researchers can identify pinned vs. rotatable uncompensated Fe and Mn spins at the interface. Concurrently, XMLD tracks how the bulk AFM Néel vector of FeMn aligns relative to the ferromagnetic layer's magnetization, revealing the microscopic mechanism behind the exchange-bias phenomenon.
* **Phase Transformations and Anisotropy:** FeMn can exhibit complex non-collinear or collinear magnetic structures depending on its crystal phase (such as the fcc $\gamma$-FeMn phase), thickness, and growth conditions. XMLD serves as a precise probe to monitor temperature-dependent phase transitions and spin-reorientation transitions within thin FeMn films.

### Conclusion

The synergy between **FeMn**, **XMCD**, and **XMLD** illustrates the power of modern X-ray spectroscopy in solving fundamental problems in magnetism. By using XMCD to capture interfacial uncompensated moments and XMLD to visualize the underlying antiferromagnetic spin axis, researchers can fully decipher the complex magnetic landscape of FeMn. These insights are crucial for pushing the boundaries of antiferromagnetic spintronics, paving the way for faster, smaller, and more energy-efficient electronic devices.
